description: "The European Commission imposed a safeguard on grain-oriented electrical steel on 18 September 2026 using tariff-rate quotas and price thresholds. Here is what those two measure types do to an importer's landed cost, and what this article cannot tell you."

    note: "Safeguard measure on grain-oriented electrical steel, imposed 18 September 2026; measure types: tariff-rate quotas and price thresholds."
---

A safeguard on grain-oriented electrical steel was imposed in the EU on **18 September 2026**. The measure, published by the European Commission's DG Trade and Economic Security, uses two instruments: **tariff-rate quotas** and **price thresholds**.

That is the whole of what the official record gives us here: a date and two measure types. This article does not have the quota volumes, the in-quota and out-of-quota duty rates, the price threshold levels, or the country allocation. It will not invent them. What it can do is explain precisely what each of those two instruments does to an importer's cost, so that when you pull the actual figures from the regulation you know which number goes where.

## Why the measure type matters more than the headline

Importers tend to read a safeguard as "a duty". It is not, necessarily. A safeguard can be structured so that most shipments pay nothing, and the cost lands only on the volume above a line, or only on goods priced below a floor. The two instruments named in this measure work in completely different ways, and they can apply to the same shipment.

Grain-oriented electrical steel is a specialised product — transformer core material — bought to a specification, often on annual contracts, often from a small number of mills. That makes the structure of the measure unusually consequential: a quota that fills early in a quota period does not raise your cost gradually, it flips your next shipment from in-quota to out-of-quota treatment.

## Tariff-rate quota: the cost is a cliff, not a slope

A tariff-rate quota splits the duty treatment of a product into two regimes:

- **Inside the quota**, the volume up to a set quantity enters at the in-quota rate.
- **Outside the quota**, volume above that quantity enters at the out-of-quota rate.

For landed-cost purposes, three things follow, and none of them are in the figures we have:

1. **The quota period.** Quotas are administered over a defined period. Your cost depends on where in that period your goods are entered, not on when you signed the contract.
2. **The allocation method.** Quota volume may be allocated to named suppliers or countries, or administered first-come-first-served. Under first-come-first-served, the quota can be exhausted before your vessel arrives, and the out-of-quota rate applies to goods you had already priced at the in-quota rate.
3. **The gap between the two rates.** The entire cost consequence of the quota is the difference between the in-quota and out-of-quota rate, multiplied by the volume above the line. Without both rates, no per-tonne figure can be computed.

The practical exposure is therefore not "the duty" but **the volume of your order that lands on the wrong side of the line**. If you buy in container or coil lots, the boundary can fall inside a single shipment.

## Price thresholds: the cost is a floor under your invoice

A price threshold works on a different variable entirely. Instead of counting volume, it tests the price at which the goods are entered. Goods entered below the threshold are treated differently from goods entered at or above it — typically by having duty assessed to bring the entry price up to the threshold, or by triggering the higher rate.

For an importer, this changes the negotiation, not just the customs entry:

- **A cheap purchase price is not automatically a cheap landed cost.** If your supplier's price sits below the threshold, the threshold — not the invoice — sets the duty base.
- **The threshold interacts with the quota.** A shipment can be inside the quota by volume and still be caught by the price test, or the reverse. You have to test both conditions for each entry.
- **Transfer pricing and related-party purchases need a second look.** Where the declared value is set by something other than an arm's-length negotiation, the threshold is the number that will be argued about.

## What to do before your next shipment

Given only the date and the measure types, the honest checklist is short and all of it is about getting the missing numbers from the regulation itself:

1. **Get the quota period and the volume.** Note the start and end of the quota period and the total quantity, and whether it is allocated by country or supplier.
2. **Get both rates.** The in-quota rate and the out-of-quota rate. The difference between them is your per-tonne exposure above the line.
3. **Get the threshold level and its basis.** What price is tested — customs value, unit price per tonne, ex-works or delivered — and what happens to an entry below it.
4. **Check your position in the quota.** If administration is first-come-first-served, ask your customs broker what the remaining balance is before you commit to a delivery date.
5. **Re-run your landed cost on both regimes.** Price the shipment as in-quota and as out-of-quota, and price it above and below the threshold. The worst case of those four is the number to put in front of your buyer.

## What this article does not contain

It does not contain the quota volume, the duty rates, the threshold level, the product scope in terms of CN codes, or the country allocation. Those are the figures that decide your cost, and they are not in the source material behind this piece. Any article that gave you a per-tonne number for this measure without citing the regulation's own figures would be making it up.

The one thing that is certain from the record is the date: **18 September 2026**. If you have grain-oriented electrical steel in transit or on order with an entry date on or after that date, the measure applies to you, and the two instruments to check are the tariff-rate quota and the price threshold.

If the quota is administered first-come-first-served, the line can be crossed before your vessel arrives, and goods you priced at the in-quota rate are entered at the out-of-quota rate. If it is allocated by country or supplier, the line is fixed to your origin.

**Price threshold — a floor under the invoice.** This tests the price at which goods are entered, not the volume. Goods entered below the threshold are treated differently from goods at or above it. A cheap purchase price is therefore not automatically a cheap landed cost: the threshold, not the invoice, sets the base. A shipment can be inside the quota by volume and still be caught by the price test, or the reverse.

## FAQ

**What exactly was imposed on 18 September 2026?**
A safeguard measure on grain-oriented electrical steel, recorded by the European Commission, DG Trade and Economic Security. The record names two measure types: tariff-rate quotas and price thresholds. It does not give the quota volume, the in-quota rate, the out-of-quota rate, the threshold level, or the country allocation. Those are the figures that determine what an importer pays, and they have to be read from the regulation itself. This article deliberately does not supply them, because a rate that is not in the source is a rate that cannot be relied on in a contract negotiation or a customs entry.

**Does a tariff-rate quota mean I pay duty on everything?**
No. A tariff-rate quota splits treatment by volume: the quantity inside the quota enters at the in-quota rate, and only volume above that line enters at the out-of-quota rate. Your cost is the difference between the two rates applied to the volume above the line. The practical risk is timing. If the quota is administered first-come-first-served, the line can be crossed before your goods are entered, and a shipment priced at the in-quota rate is assessed at the out-of-quota rate. Ask your broker for the remaining balance before you commit to a delivery date.

**How is a price threshold different from a duty rate?**
A price threshold tests the price at which goods are entered rather than the volume. Goods entered below the threshold are treated differently from goods entered at or above it. The consequence for a buyer is that a low purchase price does not guarantee a low landed cost: the threshold, not the invoice, sets the base. A shipment can be inside the quota by volume and still be caught by the price test. Where the declared value comes from a related-party or transfer-priced purchase, the threshold is the number that will be argued about at entry.

**Can I work out a per-tonne cost from this article?**
No, and that is the point of saying so. A per-tonne figure needs the in-quota rate, the out-of-quota rate, the quota volume and period, and the threshold level with its basis.
